sources.title: Estimated Use of Water in the United States in 2015
sources.coverage: United States, Puerto Rico, and U.S. Virgin Islands; withdrawals by category and source for 2015 with historical tables
sources.retained_fact: 322 Bgal/d total withdrawals; 281 Bgal/d freshwater; category, source, and historical values
sources.limitations: Latest fully comparable all-category national inventory is for 2015; withdrawal is not consumption; industrial public-supply deliveries are excluded.

sources.title: Water Availability and Use Science Program—National Estimates of Water Withdrawal and Consumptive Use for Crop Irrigation, Thermoelectric Power Generation, and Public Supply, 2010–20
sources.coverage: Conterminous United States; monthly 2010–2020 estimates for three sectors
sources.retained_fact: 2010–20 average and annual withdrawals and consumptive-use estimates for irrigation, public supply, and thermoelectric generation
sources.limitations: Not an update of every Circular 1441 category; modeled geography and allocation differ from the 2015 inventory.

sources.title: New nationwide tool helps answer: Do we have enough water?
sources.retained_fact: Nearly 27 million people—about 8 percent—live where water demand consistently approaches or exceeds natural supply
sources.limitations: National stress screening is not a utility reliability forecast or a city failure date.

sources.title: National Water Availability Assessment Data Catalog
sources.coverage: National supply, demand, and availability data products
sources.retained_fact: Machine-access route for watershed-level dashboard layers
sources.limitations: Individual products require their own variable, period, and spatial-unit metadata.

sources.title: Water-level and recoverable water in storage changes, High Plains aquifer, predevelopment to 2019 and 2017–19
sources.retained_fact: 2.91 billion acre-feet recoverable storage in 2019 and 286.4 million acre-feet decline since predevelopment
sources.limitations: Basin-wide remaining volume does not describe local saturated thickness or economic well viability.

sources.title: Future agricultural production and groundwater sustainability from the Ogallala Aquifer
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Agriculture Agricultural Research Service
sources.coverage: High Plains aquifer irrigated agriculture through 2100
sources.retained_fact: Modeled 24 percent of current irrigated area unable to support irrigation by 2100
sources.limitations: Scenario/model result for agricultural viability, not aquifer-wide physical exhaustion.

sources.title: 2027 State Water Plan
sources.coverage: Texas, 2030–2080 planning decades under drought-of-record conditions
sources.retained_fact: Existing supply declines, potential shortage grows from 3.6 to 5.8 million acre-feet absent recommended strategies
sources.limitations: Planning counterfactual; adopted strategies are intended to prevent or reduce shortages.

sources.title: 2026 Region O Llano Estacado Regional Water Plan
sources.retained_fact: Hale County existing supply declines from 123,819 acre-feet/year in 2030 to 29,691 in 2080
sources.limitations: Planning supply estimate under plan assumptions; does not mean all county wells fail.

sources.title: New Mexico 50-Year Water Action Plan rulemaking and technical record
sources.publisher: New Mexico Office of the State Engineer
sources.retained_fact: Planning basis of roughly 25 percent less water in rivers and aquifers and an approximately 750,000 acre-foot shortfall
sources.limitations: State planning estimate with uncertainty; timing and impacts differ by basin and depend on management.

sources.title: Fifth National Climate Assessment, Chapter 4: Water
sources.coverage: United States water cycle, supply, demand, quality, and infrastructure
sources.retained_fact: Groundwater decline, altered runoff, rising irrigation demand, and interacting climate and management risks
sources.limitations: National synthesis; local dates require basin and utility sources.

sources.title: Colorado River Post-2026 Operations
sources.retained_fact: New operating rules are required for water year 2027; draft EIS issued January 2026 without a preferred alternative
sources.limitations: Pending decision; alternatives are not predictions and allocations remain legally and politically contested.

sources.title: Colorado River Basin Water Supply and Demand Study
sources.retained_fact: Legacy scenario analysis reported a median 3.2 million acre-foot supply-demand imbalance by 2060
sources.limitations: Legacy scenario, not the current post-2026 operating forecast.

sources.title: Industrial Water Use
sources.retained_fact: 14.8 Bgal/d self-supplied industrial withdrawals, 14.0 Bgal/d freshwater, 82 percent surface water
sources.limitations: Excludes industrial water delivered by public suppliers and does not isolate plastics.

sources.title: NAICS 325211—Plastics Material and Resin Manufacturing
sources.retained_fact: Defines a relevant but incomplete plastics-production industry boundary
sources.limitations: Economic classification does not supply direct water withdrawals or consumption.

sources.title: NAICS 326—Plastics and Rubber Products Manufacturing
sources.coverage: U.S. plastics and rubber product establishments
sources.retained_fact: Defines downstream converting/product manufacturing boundary
sources.limitations: Combines plastics and rubber at sector level and does not provide a national water balance.

sources.title: Development Document for Effluent Limitations Guidelines: Organic Chemicals, Plastics and Synthetic Fibers
sources.coverage: 406 surveyed U.S. organic chemical, plastics, and synthetic-fiber plants
sources.retained_fact: 5,677 Mgal/d intake, of which 4,765 Mgal/d was noncontact cooling
sources.limitations: Historical, mixed-industry, gross-intake survey; not current plastics-only consumption.

sources.title: Life Cycle Environmental Impacts of Plastics: A Review
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.retained_fact: Documents data and methodological gaps including geography, additives, and allocation
sources.limitations: Review does not provide one authoritative national plastics-water total.

sources.title: Variability in life cycle inventory data for plastics
sources.coverage: PET, HDPE, PP, bio-PE, and PLA production inventories
sources.retained_fact: Water-consumption results vary materially among GREET, USLCI, ecoinvent, and GaBi inventories
sources.limitations: Production-stage comparison is not a full product, use, end-of-life, or scarcity-weighted assessment.

sources.title: Federal LCA Commons
sources.retained_fact: Candidate source for future resin, substitute, energy, and end-of-life inventories
sources.limitations: Datasets require harmonization of system boundaries, geography, time, and allocation.

sources.title: 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report
sources.coverage: U.S. data centers, historical through 2023 and projections to 2028
sources.retained_fact: 66 billion liters direct water in 2023; electricity and water projections through 2028
sources.limitations: Projection depends on uncertain AI demand, deployment, cooling, and efficiency.

sources.title: Avoiding waste heat through AI data center design
sources.coverage: U.S. data-center direct water scenarios to 2028
sources.retained_fact: Total direct water projected at 0.14–0.28 billion cubic meters in 2028
sources.limitations: Scenario range, not a guaranteed demand value.

sources.title: Water use of data center workloads: A review and harmonization of metrics
sources.retained_fact: Reported workload water use varies by more than four orders of magnitude with site, grid, cooling, and workload
sources.limitations: Cannot be reduced to one water-per-query coefficient.

sources.title: About WaterSense
sources.coverage: U.S. residential water use and efficiency
sources.retained_fact: Average household use equivalent of 82 gallons per person per day; outdoor and leak context
sources.limitations: Program summary values are national averages, not local utility demand.

sources.title: Phoenix Active Management Area Groundwater Supply Updates
sources.coverage: Phoenix Active Management Area, 100-year assured-water-supply horizon
sources.retained_fact: Model shows 4.86 million acre-feet of unmet groundwater demand and constrains new groundwater-based determinations
sources.limitations: AMA is larger than the City of Phoenix; model does not say the city utility runs out and existing homeowners retain protections.

sources.title: Phoenix Water Services: About Us
sources.coverage: City of Phoenix retail water system
sources.retained_fact: Approximately 97–99 percent surface water and roughly 2 percent groundwater in the cited operating profile
sources.limitations: Annual mix varies and legal accounting differs from physical delivery.

sources.title: Where Your Water Comes From
sources.retained_fact: Approximately 90 percent Colorado River water and 10 percent local groundwater
sources.limitations: Regional supply mix, not every local purveyor or year.

sources.title: Drinking Water Distribution System
sources.retained_fact: Delivered water enters through wells, including recovered Colorado River water recharged into the aquifer
sources.limitations: Physical well delivery should not be mislabeled as purely native groundwater.

sources.title: Our Aquifers
sources.retained_fact: In a normal year about half of supply is from the Hueco and Mesilla Bolson aquifers
sources.limitations: Annual proportions vary with Rio Grande supply and operations.

sources.title: El Paso Water FY 2024–25 Budget Book
sources.retained_fact: 44 percent Rio Grande, 36 percent Hueco Bolson, and 20 percent Mesilla Bolson
sources.limitations: Single-year mix.

sources.title: Your Drinking Water
sources.publisher: Albuquerque Bernalillo County Water Utility Authority
sources.retained_fact: San Juan–Chama surface water and Santa Fe Group aquifer are jointly managed
sources.limitations: Portfolio and pumping vary by year.

sources.title: 2025 Drinking Water Quality Report
sources.publisher: Los Angeles Department of Water and Power
sources.retained_fact: 44 percent Los Angeles Aqueduct, 52 percent Metropolitan Water District, 1 percent local groundwater, 3 percent recycled water
sources.limitations: Single-year portfolio; MWD water combines Colorado River and State Water Project sources.

sources.title: Your Water
sources.retained_fact: Diversified imported Colorado River, Northern California, local, recycled, and desalinated supplies
sources.limitations: Mix varies by hydrology and contract year.

sources.title: Seawater Desalination
sources.retained_fact: 50 Mgal/d product capacity, 56,000 acre-feet/year, approximately 7–10 percent of regional demand, about 400,000 people
sources.limitations: Capacity and equivalence are regional planning values, not constant output.

sources.title: Water Quality Information
sources.retained_fact: Surface reservoirs and connected rivers supply the system; no groundwater source is used
sources.limitations: Reliability depends on the larger regional reservoir and conveyance portfolio.

sources.title: Houston Water Capital Improvement Plan
sources.retained_fact: Supply portfolio approximately 86 percent surface water and 14 percent groundwater
sources.limitations: Planning profile, not a fixed annual mix.

sources.title: Edwards Aquifer
sources.retained_fact: Edwards Aquifer supplied approximately 47 percent in 2025 within a diversified portfolio
sources.limitations: Annual mix and pumping restrictions vary.

sources.title: Saltwater Intrusion
sources.retained_fact: Biscayne aquifer is the primary source and is vulnerable to saltwater intrusion
sources.limitations: Vulnerability does not by itself specify the date or magnitude of wellfield impacts.

sources.title: Hydrologic conditions that control saltwater intrusion in southeast Florida
sources.retained_fact: Canal stages, drainage, pumping, and drought control intrusion; sea-level rise can aggravate it
sources.limitations: Local hydrogeology and management determine wellfield exposure.

sources.title: Miami-Dade County saltwater intrusion model status memorandum
sources.retained_fact: Modeled wellfields were not impacted through 2040 even under the evaluated high sea-level-rise case
sources.limitations: A model result with a 2040 horizon; not evidence of safety after 2040 or under all pumping and canal conditions.

sources.title: Groundwater Sustainability of the Long Island Aquifer System
sources.coverage: Long Island, New York aquifer system
sources.retained_fact: About 2.8 million people rely on roughly 400 Mgal/d from approximately 1,500 wells; localized saltwater intrusion exists
sources.limitations: Localized well and plume risks differ from island-wide storage.

sources.title: Groundwater Monitoring Program, Brunswick–Glynn County Area, Georgia
sources.retained_fact: Documented chloride contamination exceeding 2,000 mg/L in part of the aquifer system
sources.limitations: Local industrial/pumping history; not representative of all coastal aquifers.

sources.title: Saltwater intrusion in coastal regions of North America
sources.publisher: Hydrogeology Journal / U.S. Geological Survey authors
sources.retained_fact: Intrusion pathways and severity vary from individual wells to regional closures; pumping is a central driver
sources.limitations: No universal sea-level-to-intrusion date can be transferred among aquifers.

sources.title: Drinking Water
sources.retained_fact: Potomac River water treated by the Washington Aqueduct supplies the system
sources.limitations: Source dependence is a resilience risk, not evidence of current shortage.

sources.title: DC Water unveils Pure Water DC
sources.retained_fact: Purified-water initiative is intended to reduce single-source vulnerability
sources.limitations: Program development, not completed replacement capacity.

sources.title: Drinking Water Purification
sources.publisher: Sewerage and Water Board of New Orleans
sources.retained_fact: Mississippi River is the drinking-water source
sources.limitations: Does not quantify future salt-wedge frequency or permanence.

sources.title: Saltwater Wedge
sources.publisher: Sewerage and Water Board of New Orleans
sources.retained_fact: The 2023 wedge was an episodic low-flow risk and did not reach New Orleans intakes during the posted event
sources.limitations: Incident status is not a forecast of future low-flow events.

sources.title: 2024 New York City Drinking Water Supply and Quality Report
sources.publisher: New York City Department of Environmental Protection
sources.coverage: New York City regional reservoir system
sources.retained_fact: Approximately 1 Bgal/d serves more than 9 million people from upstate watersheds
sources.limitations: System-wide profile; individual reservoirs, tunnels, and drought rules matter.

sources.title: Tampa Bay Regional Water Supply: Water Sources
sources.retained_fact: Blended river, groundwater, and desalinated seawater portfolio
sources.limitations: Facility capacities are not equal to annual production.

sources.title: Tampa Bay Seawater Desalination
sources.retained_fact: 25 Mgal/d product capacity from approximately 44 Mgal/d intake, up to roughly 10 percent of regional supply
sources.limitations: Capacity and share vary with operations and regional demand.

sources.title: Studies begin on future water projects
sources.coverage: Tampa Bay regional demand and supply planning
sources.retained_fact: Planning evaluates 10–20 Mgal/d by 2033 and an additional 25 Mgal/d by 2043
sources.limitations: Study targets, not committed project yields.

sources.title: Stage 3 Drought Restrictions
sources.retained_fact: Stage 3 restrictions and current reservoir status
sources.limitations: Volatile operational snapshot; must be refreshed before dashboard publication.

sources.title: Desalination Basics
sources.retained_fact: More than two-thirds of U.S. desalination plants use reverse osmosis to treat brackish groundwater; energy and concentrate are key constraints
sources.limitations: Technology overview, not a site-specific cost or yield estimate.

sources.title: National Brackish Groundwater Assessment
sources.coverage: U.S. brackish groundwater and desalination facilities
sources.retained_fact: 2010 inventory listed 649 facilities with 402 Mgal/d capacity; 95 percent were inland
sources.limitations: Facility count/capacity are historical and should not be presented as current inventory.

sources.title: Desalination
sources.publisher: U.S. Geological Survey Water Science School
sources.retained_fact: Approximately 270 Mgal/d of saline water used for public supply, less than 1 percent of total public-supply withdrawals
sources.limitations: Saline withdrawal is not finished product-water yield.

sources.title: Desalination Resource Management Strategy
sources.retained_fact: Brackish desalination goals add 28,000 acre-feet/year by 2030 and 84,000 by 2040; barriers include cost, energy, brine, permitting, environment, and equity
sources.limitations: Goals and potential, not guaranteed capacity.

sources.title: Kay Bailey Hutchison Desalination Plant Fact Sheet
sources.retained_fact: Up to 27.5 Mgal/d fresh-water production and deep-well concentrate disposal
sources.limitations: Site-specific geology and concentrate disposal cannot be assumed elsewhere.

sources.title: Tampa Bay Seawater Desalination Plant Expansion
sources.retained_fact: Evaluated 10.4 Mgal/d expansion, $310–365 million capital estimate, and $8.56 per thousand gallons planning cost
sources.limitations: Pre-project planning estimate subject to design, financing, energy, and permitting changes.

sources.title: The role of desalination in an increasingly water-scarce world
sources.coverage: U.S. seawater reverse-osmosis energy and deployment scenarios
sources.retained_fact: Installed seawater reverse-osmosis systems generally use 3.2–4.5 kWh per cubic meter
sources.limitations: Electricity interval is not total lifecycle energy or a universal site cost.

sources.title: Global potential for harvesting drinking water from air using solar energy
sources.coverage: Hypothetical solar atmospheric-water harvesting for drinking-water access
sources.retained_fact: Modeled one-square-meter devices with 0.2–2.5 L/kWh at 30–90 percent relative humidity against a 5 L/person/day target
sources.limitations: Development target and global potential model, not commercial utility-scale performance; authors disclosed Alphabet patent interests.

sources.title: Atmospheric Water Generation Technology Technical Brief
sources.retained_fact: Home units roughly 1–20 L/day; commercial units approximately 1,000 to over 10,000 L/day; output strongly depends on temperature and humidity
sources.limitations: Rated outputs may reflect favorable conditions and require treatment and maintenance.

sources.title: Real-world evaluation of atmospheric water generation for potable use
sources.retained_fact: Observed heterotrophic bacteria and evidence of opportunistic pathogens support downstream disinfection and management
sources.limitations: Specific tested systems and conditions; does not characterize every design.

sources.title: Dehumidifiers Key Product Criteria
sources.retained_fact: Minimum criteria span approximately 1.70–3.81 L/kWh by class
sources.limitations: Used only as a transparent condenser-efficiency proxy; dehumidifiers are not certified potable AWGs.

sources.title: Domestic water quantity, service level and health, second edition
sources.coverage: Household water quantities for health and access
sources.retained_fact: Approximately 5.3 L/person/day for drinking and about 20 L/person/day often sufficient for drinking, cooking, and basic hand/face hygiene
sources.limitations: Basic-needs guidance is not equivalent to contemporary U.S. household water demand.
